#1208. Author or artificial intelligence? Literature in crisis

AI is a hot topic at this year's Frankfurt Book Fair. An international literary scandal has raised questions about machine-generated texts.

It's the hot-button topic at the Frankfurt Book Fair: How profoundly will artificial intelligence (AI) transform the book industry, and how can this transformation be regulated?

Given the warnings about the technology's long-term risks to humanity as a whole, such debates might appear rather narrow in scope. In reality, however, they concern very concrete issues — copyright protection, the power of tech giants and the future of creativity. Many agree that the political measures taken don't go far enough.

This year, however, another aspect has entered the debate: Can we actually recognize when a text has been written with the help of artificial intelligence, and if so, can this be proven?

These are some of the questions raised by the current scandal surrounding Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien and his debut novel, "C'etait ca ou mourir," (This title means "It Was Either That or Die" in English but an English translation has not yet been published), which was published in Canada in the spring.

The book about global migration was universally acclaimed, with translation rights sold in more than 20 languages. Soon after the book was published in France, it was long-listed for the prestigious Prix Goncourt.

But then, all of a sudden, allegations emerged that the book had been written almost entirely using AI. Orelien, a rising literary star, found himself branded a fraud despite denying all the allegations. His nomination for the Goncourt was withdrawn.

So, who should we believe? An author or an AI that claims to have identified AI-generated writing?

"We will have to learn to live with doubt," said Hannes Bajohr, a professor of German literature at the University of California, Berkeley.

Bajohr has spent years examining how AI is changing both writing and reading. His prediction: If the origins of texts can no longer be reliably established, we will have to evaluate them differently. What matters will be their quality alone, rather than whether AI was used in the writing process.

Nina George, a bestselling author and the honorary president of the European Writers' Council, is unwilling to accept this.

At the Frankfurt Book Fair, she was awarded the Friedrich Perthes Prize in recognition of her commitment to issues such as AI and copyright reform.

George has addressed the European Parliament and the lower house of the German parliament, speaking and writing tirelessly about the dangers of AI models. It is perverse, she said, that an author should suddenly have to prove that their writing is the creation of a human. The focus of her campaigns are the tech corporations' self-serving mentality and copyright protection.

But what if an author sees AI not as an enemy but as a tool that makes writing easier?

US author and artist Luke Stoffel deliberately used AI in his memoir, "How To Win One Million Dollars and Shit Glitter," and was open about doing so.

"I'm dyslexic," he said in a video interview. "I've always written and made up stories, but I never dared to take them any further."

It was only with the help of AI, he said, that he was able to fulfill his dream. The technology drew his attention to weaknesses in his writing and suggested a marketing strategy that actually worked.

In May 2026, he received an award from the Independent Book Publishers Association for the book.

For South African author Coral Hart, AI is actually the foundation of her business model. Publishing under various pseudonyms, each year she releases more than 200 different novels, spanning the genres of romance, thriller and mystery.

Hart sees herself as an ideas person, as well as an editor and publisher. Although none of her books has yet become a bestseller, the business is profitable, she said, adding that each book reaches more than 5,000 people.

Stoffel considers the entire debate hypocritical and points out that many publishers have been working with AI tools for some time. He's certain that "right now, a million-copy bestseller is being printed that was created with the help of AI. The author won't admit it, and then there'll be a scandal."

It is entirely possible that the scandal surrounding Thelyson Orelien is precisely that story. But we may never know for sure.

For now, the battle against the tech giants continues, some of which are themselves increasingly concerned about losing control.

At the very start of the Frankfurt fair, the German Publishers and Booksellers Association issued an appeal to policymakers in Berlin and Brussels, calling for stricter regulation of artificial intelligence, which they said is more urgent than ever. More than 140 publishers have signed it.

But for now, it remains just an appeal. And the question of what authors themselves should be permitted to do with AI will undoubtedly continue to fuel debates in the future.

#1206. Hibs boss insists his improving team are ready to upset the odds against Rangers in cup final

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 14:00 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 15:31 EDT, 1 November 2026

Marink Reedijk warned Rangers that they'll face an ever-improving Hibs team when they meet in the Premier Sports Cup Final next month.

The Dutchman created history by becoming the first manager of the Easter Road club to taste a Hampden victory over Hearts when they came from behind to win 2-1.

After recording just one draw in his four opening league games, Reedijk was starting to feel the heat ahead of the semi-final.

But having secured a date against Rangers on December 13, the Leith boss feels his side are now in a different place.

Asked what gave him the confidence that his side can now upset the odds and win the cup for the first time since 2007, Reedijk said: 'The performance of today and the performance we showed the week before.

'And if we have more progression, we can make every opponent's lives a little bit difficult or very difficult.

Hibs boss Marink Reedijk celebrates his team's 2-1 win over Hearts with Josh Mulligan

'And no matter which team it is, it's always another match to play.

'Finals are, again, special matches, but also finals are not only based on these special moments.

'It's also about teams with a plan and teams with an idea.

'And I think if we build on what we are doing now, keep on going - it will have ups and downs - I know I have a really good belief that we also can do something in the final.'

Behind when Claudio Braga struck on four minutes, Hibs responded brilliantly and deservedly went in ahead at the break thanks to goals from Martin Boyle and Jamie McGrath.

Reedijk was effusive in his praise for the way his players bounced back from the early blow to dominate the game.

'In the first half, I really enjoyed how we played football, how we dominated the game on the ball, how we made sure that we created chances and gave Hearts a big problem in defence,' he reflected.

'And in the second half, I really enjoyed the togetherness, the work rate, the energy, the desire.

The Hibs players start the party after reaching League Cup final by beating Hearts

'This is where we made a big step today. And also I'm so happy for the staff, the players, because they worked so hard for this. And that's really important.

'Not only those people, like the staff and the players, but also for the fans who kept on supporting us, not only during the match, but especially those matches where we didn't have the result like it was today. And that's really important to me.

Reedijk was asked if his first victory at the fifth attempt was the first real sign that the players had bought into what he was trying to do.

'Not the first sign,' he stressed. 'For me, I already saw glimpses and signs in the last matches, starting at Falkirk, where you see that we dominated the game, but we didn't bring the game home and lost by individual errors and moments.

'And then against Celtic and St Mirren also you saw that we can dominate matches, that we can make our way of playing a challenge for the opponent. That didn't lead to the result we wanted.

'However, today it did. So, it is not the first sign, but it is the first performance with a result.'

Jamie McGrath soaks up the acclaim after putting Hibernian in front at Hampden

At full time, the entire Hibs squad lapped up the rendition of Sunshine on Leith which was sung by their supporters.

Reedijk admitted that he felt more emotional at the scenes than his impassive demeanour suggested.

'I'm not always showing my emotions, but it's really touching,' he said.

'Maybe it looks like I'm an ice king, so to say.

'Normally in Holland we say ice queen, but therefore an ice king because I'm not a woman.

'But for me, it is really important that this happens and it comes close to my heart because this is what football is about.

'Guys who inspire people on the pitch with something people off the pitch and in the stands love to see.

#1204. Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Tandem repeats (TRs)—highly polymorphic, repetitive sequences across the human genome—are important regulators of gene expression but remain underexplored due to challenges in accurate genotyping and analysis1. Here we generate whole-genome and single-cell RNA sequencing from more than 5.4 million blood-derived cells across 1,925 individuals in two cohorts2, and perform meta-analysis to characterize the impact of variation in more than 1.7 million TR loci on immune cell type-specific gene expression. We identify more than 69,000 single-cell expression quantitative trait loci, 30.7% of which are specific to 1 of 28 immune cell types, and reveal dynamic regulatory effects using cell-state inference. Matched single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with high-throughput sequencing profiles from more than 3.4 million nuclei in 922 individuals3 uncover chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci for nearly one-third of expression-associated TRs, supporting coordinated effects on cis-regulatory architecture. Fine-mapping implicates 1,490 TRs as candidate causal drivers of gene expression in 6.1% of tested genes, and colocalization analyses highlight more than 200 genes in which TRs likely mediate genetic associations with immune and haematological traits. Together, these results provide a genome-wide, multiomic view of TR-mediated regulation in the human immune system, establishing TRs as key contributors to cell type-specific regulatory variation and complex trait architecture.

a, Distribution of number of distinct alleles per locus. b, Distribution of mode allele per locus. c, Distribution of summed alleles (of a diploid genotype). X-axis truncated at 100 repeats. Overall, 13.7% of alleles represented expansions relative to the locus-specific mode, 9.3% were contractions, and the remainder matched the mode allele exactly. The median summed dosage across all loci was 14 repeat units. Following stringent filtering for call quality and locus-level metrics (Methods), the resulting high-confidence callset had a median of 6 distinct alleles per locus and a median mode allele length of 9 repeats.

Bulk eTR catalogs were based on GTEx11,36 (bulk RNA-seq of whole blood; FDR < 10% for STRs and <5% for VNTRs) and gEUVADIS96 (bulk RNA-seq of HapMap lymphoblastoid cell lines; FDR < 5%) datasets. Differences in cell type/tissue resolution, TR genotyping methods, and analysis pipelines limit interpretability of direct comparisons. In particular, cell type-specific signals discovered in TenK10K Phase 1 may be diluted in bulk tissue, and TR catalogs used in prior studies may not capture loci genotyped in TenK10K Phase 1.

#1203. 'Ragebait' is the 2026 German Youth Word of the Year

Already named the 2025 Oxford Word of the Year, "rage bait" has also been widely adopted in German slang.

The 2026 Youth Word of the Year, "Ragebait," was announced on Saturday at the Frankfurt Book Fair by publisher PONS Langenscheidt.

The "Jugendwort des Jahres," or German Youth Word of the Year, is an annual campaign that documents the popularity of new slang expressions.

"Ragebait" (in English: rage bait) refers to social media content that is deliberately designed to make people angry, frustrated or morally outraged.

It aims to drive engagement, since the algorithms of platforms like Instagram, TikTok and X reward high-energy interaction. A post that generates a heated debate through angry comments, or that is widely shared due to the emotional reaction it provokes, counts as high engagement, which leads the platforms to push the content to more feeds.

"Ragebait" was on a shortlist of three words for the 2026 Youth Word of the Year, alongside "Peak" and "Crashout."

All three terms are borrowed from English, demonstrating once again the language's significant influence on German youth culture.

Around 1 million young people, aged 11 to 20, have voted since August 28 for their favorite term.

"Ragebait" obtained 36.5% of the votes, followed by 33.8% for "Peak" and 29.7% for "Crashout."

"The close result shows that all three terms have a firm place in the vocabulary of generations Z and Alpha," said Artur Raiser, marketing manager at PONS Langenscheidt, in a press statement. "'Ragebait' held a slight lead from the start," but only by a narrow margin throughout the voting period, he added.

"It remained an exciting race for us at the publishing house, too, until the very last moment," said Raiser

"Crashout" (used by young Germans as "crashout gehen," or "going crash out") originally comes from the English "to crash out," which traditionally means to fall asleep very quickly due to exhaustion.

But in newer internet slang, popularized on gaming and social media platforms, "crashing out" means having an intense emotional breakdown, losing control of one's temper or reacting with sudden, uncontrolled anger or stress. It is often used with a touch of humor, to emphasize that the reaction might be somewhat exaggerated.

As for the other shortlisted word, "Peak," it refers to something that is the absolute best. In German youth slang, it functions like an adjective: "That was peak football" or "that is peak comedy."

PONS Langenscheidt, a publishing company that specializes in language reference works, has been selecting the German Youth Word of the Year since 2008 — originally via a jury, and since 2020 through an online vote. Offensive, racist or discriminatory terms are not permitted. The multi-stage public nomination and voting process for next year's word will start in the summer of 2027.

"Das crazy" was selected last year, while "Aura" was the Youth Word of the Year 2024.

This article was originally written in German.

#1201. UK students call for school uniforms to be banned in pornography

Short skirts, knee-high socks, white blouses: Girls' school uniform items are widely used as costumes in pornographic videos. As students experience harassment, a group wants to change that.

Aylin and Mae, both age 15, are members of their school's Little Feminist Book Club in Bicester, Oxfordshire, England.

During a group discussion, the club learned that teenagers at other schools were trying to have the sale of school uniforms banned in sex shops.

Schoolgirl costumes are also widely used in pornographic videos.

"All of us unanimously agreed. We wanted to take it a step further; we wanted to ban school uniform from all pornography," Aylin told DW. As a result, they started a petition to raise awareness of the issue.

Many of their fellow students, as the petition states, have already had unpleasant experiences while wearing their uniforms. Some reported being harassed as early as the age of 11. Many of these experiences had left them feeling frightened, ashamed and insecure. "I don't wear my school uniform outside of school," said Mae. "I don't like wearing it out."

In their petition, the girls also refer to a 2018 report by the charity Plan International. According to a survey in the report, 35% of the 1,004 respondents aged 14 to 21 had experienced unwanted sexual attention while wearing a school uniform. Eight percent said they had been filmed or photographed by a stranger without their permission, or that someone had taken a photo under their school skirt, known as "upskirting."

"Something that should actually be innocent, something that is supposed to symbolize a community, has now become discredited in society," said Mae. "And our perception of what a school uniform represents has been distorted by this disgusting media."

School uniforms are common in many countries around the world. They are meant to make class and financial divides less visible, which is also supposed to prevent bullying while strengthening a community feeling.

In the United Kingdom, uniforms are mandatory at almost all schools and preschools, which means essentially all children between the ages of 4 to 16 wear them.

Outside school, children have no way to escape unwanted attention.

"We just want to prevent people from thinking about children and school uniforms in that way," said Mae. "Hopefully, we'll be able to actually turn the ban into legislation."

Until that happens, they still have a long way to go, but the girls are optimistic. As of October 5, 2026, the petition has garnered more than 24,000 signatures. Thanks to an article in the English newspaper The Times, it's also gotten plenty of attention.

Now, Mae and Aylin hope to get parliament to debate the issue. Two Members of Parliament have already voiced their support.

But the girls also know some people believe longer skirts are the solution. "I believe that's wrong," explains Aylin. "We shouldn't blame the victims. We should blame those who think it is acceptable to sexualize them."

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 15:31 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 15:31 EDT, 1 November 2026

Wouter Vrancken claimed Hearts were unable to cope with the double blow of losing Tomas Magnusson and Calvin Miller as their hopes of lifting the Premier Sports Cup ended with a 2-1 defeat by Hibs.

Already missing eight first-team players, the Tynecastle men were further depleted when the pair left the field inside the opening 38 minutes of their semi-final at Hampden.

Vrancken felt the loss of two more key players was instrumental in his side failing to build on the early lead handed to them by Claudio Braga.

Instead, Hibs hit back with goals by Martin Boyle and Jamie McGrath to secure a place in next month's final against Rangers.

'I'm really sore and disappointed, of course, especially when you see how the game was going,' said Vrancken.

'It didn't have to go that way because we had control with how we started.

Wouter Vrancken insists Hearts had control until two key players left the field with injuries

Tomas Magnusson is treated for a head knock that led to his substitution early in the semi-final

Calvin Miller uses crutches after going off with what appeared to be a knee injury at Hampden

'But it changed the moment Tomas was injured, that's clear. And then afterwards with Cal.

'I'm not pointing out the guys who came out, but those changes took us out of our rhythm.

'We lost some connections and weren't top in the duels. At first, we were picking up second balls and finding the right spaces.

'But then we lost those profiles and we were searching again. There were hesitations and that gave Hibs too much space.

'You lose the game in that 20 minutes. At half-time, we tried to make adjustments, be clear and try to take those hesitations out.

'It was much better and we dominated the game again.

'Unfortunately, we didn't get rewarded. The players have taken a lot of knocks mentally and emotionally so you just hope they get rewarded for fighting hard.

'It's a pity they didn't especially in such a game.'

Magnusson came off with a head-knock while Miller succumbed to what appeared to be a knee injury.

'I haven't seen Tomas because he's at hospital,' Vrancken explained.

'Calvin is in a brace, but it's difficult to say. We have to wait for a scan tomorrow.

'With Tomas, the medical staff did a concussion test on the pitch at that moment.

'He passed it but when he came to me, he was going from left to right and couldn't stand on his legs any more.

'When I saw that, there was no doubt in my head about letting him back on the pitch. He said, I can't do it.'

Vrancken now faces serious selection issues for the Conference League match away to Swiss side Thun on Thursday.

'I don't know how I make changes. We'll see how it goes and who's fit,' he said.

'Players will have to play out of position, so we'll see who has the quality to play in certain ones.

'We have to make the puzzle on Monday or Tuesday.

'And we have to keep pushing the guys because when you go on the pitch, there can be no excuses, you have to take responsibility, go for it and try to win the game.

'We have 10 out. When you have those 10, you have a really good squad in the Premiership.

'The players have taken responsibility in difficult moments, like dominating parts of the game today.

'When they do that, you just hope they reward themselves like they did today in the second half. It's just a pity the last 20 minutes of the first half which killed the game.

'Everyone is disappointed, no matter the situation we're in.

'When you see the second half, you know there was something in the game today even with the knocks we got.

'So, the disappointment is really big, not about losing players, but missing the chance to beat your rivals and go to the final.'

#1198. How green is Europe's urban public transport? A data-driven reality check

Greener buses and cleaner fleets are reshaping public transport across Europe. But are cities moving fast enough to meet their zero-emission goals?

An electric plug icon on their windows makes them easy to spot in cities like Brussels and Madrid. Quietly navigating the streets, electric buses have become an increasingly common sight on Europe's streets in recent years.

Michela Le Pira, assistant professor of transportation at Italy's University of Catania, says removing tailpipe emissions — the gases and particles generated when a combustion vehicle is running — might be "the easiest strategy to improve public transport."

Most Europeans live in urban settings, and road transport harms air quality. In 2023, almost 300,000 deaths across the EU were caused by air pollution levels exceeding the World Health Organization's (WHO) recommended thresholds.

Of all fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations in European urban areas, about 14% come from road transport, including public, private and freight transport. Additionally, towns and cities account for nearly a quarter of the European Union's transport greenhouse gas emissions (GHG).

DW and the European Data Journalism Network evaluated more than a decade's worth of data from more than 100 reports and sources on public transit and the emissions it causes, and identified 148 sustainability commitments by local authorities and transport operators in 33 cities across Europe. The analysis focuses on motorized mass transit, leaving out bikes and pedestrians as well as taxis, shared vehicles and e-scooters.

The EU wants to become the first climate-neutral continent by 2050. A key part of that plan is cutting transport-related GHG emissions by 90% from 1990 levels.

As DW's analysis shows, Copenhagen is the only EU capital that has almost electrified its entire bus fleet — its vehicles do not have combustion engines and therefore do not produce tailpipe emissions. In cities like Rome, Lisbon and Nicosia, more than 90% of buses still run on diesel, and metros and trams account for less than 10% of their public transport fleet.

Although cars still dominate European streets, "electric buses are one way to reduce local air pollution," said Martin Baierl, data analyst with Transport & Environment, an advocacy non-profit for clean transport.

EU funds enabled many cities to increase their electric and alternative fuel bus fleets from 2021 on.

Electric buses comprise 20% of the total fleet in EU capitals and selected cities. Their number increased by 55% between 2021 and 2025 — equivalent to 1,234 more such vehicles on the road. The number of diesel-only buses has been declining since then, although they still outnumber those running on alternative fuel.

In addition to decarbonizing the bus fleet and helping to reduce air pollution, embracing electric models can help to lower noise and public transport operating costs. All the more so if the city produces its own electricity, explains Baierl. However, the outlay for e-buses is higher than for diesel models. In 20 out of the 31 cities with data to analyze, over 50% of the bus fleet is made up of traditional vehicles.

Brussels, for example, was an early adopter of moving away from traditional diesel-powered buses, switching to hybrids instead. Now the Belgian capital is in the process of electrifying its fleet, but at a slower pace. "It's not easy to know what the right technology will be in the end," Baierl said.

Another example is hydrogen-powered buses, which also produce zero emissions but are more costly to operate than their electric counterparts.

Transportation is the only major sector where greenhouse gas emissions remain above 1990 levels, despite the EU's ambition of a 90% reduction by 2050.

On average, public transport — including buses, trams and metros — is used for more than a quarter of trips in the 10 largest EU capitals, according to recent data from the non-profit group CDP (formerly the Carbon Disclosure Project). In Stockholm, the share is 49%, while in the smaller Slovenian capital of Ljubljana, it's 11%. DW analysis of transport sustainability pledges reveals that only four cities have explicitly committed to achieving zero emissions in buses or all public transport.

Yannis Papadimitriou lives 85 kilometers (about 53 miles) away from Athens, the EU capital with the highest air pollution mortality risk. He travels to work by commuter rail, a means of transport he'd like to see promoted more.

"For me it is a very conscious choice to use electric public transport, especially trains, which are the safest, most environmentally friendly and quickest way of transport."

Though trains, trams and metros run on electricity, there are more buses within city boundaries, and in many urban areas the majority still run on diesel.

In Northern Europe, 15 kilometers away from Copenhagen, Poul Kattler also used to commute to work. He is now retired and takes the bus more frequently with his grandchildren. Despite Copenhagen having an almost completely fossil-fuel-free public transport system (only one bus runs on biomethane), the metro expansion, which is responding to the city's growth, comes with its own set of concerns.

"The whole construction phase [of the new metro line] is extremely environmentally demanding," Kattler said. If the construction emissions are considered, "the CO2 balance would be very poor for the metro now."

But in the long run, the benefits of a new metro line in reducing CO2 emissions outweigh its construction-related emissions, Le Pira said.

Combustion or exhaust emissions are not the only way transport pollutes the air and the environment. Indirect emissions, like those coming from electricity generation or fuel production, add to transport's CO2 footprint. Brakes and wheels release non-exhaust particle matter when wagons or vehicles slow down.

Since 1992, buses and any vehicle running on fossil fuels in the EU have been subject to stricter emissions standards. Fine particle emissions from buses and heavy-duty vehicles had dropped by 92% in 2022 according to the European Environment Agency. Yet overall road transport non-exhaust emissions from tire wear have increased 58% in two decades, as cars have become heavier.

With a few exceptions, EU member states are not close to cutting greenhouse gas transport emissions by 90%, as envisioned by the EU's 2050 target.

Zero-emission public transport is one step toward decarbonizing transport in cities and meeting GHG reduction goals. The next challenge is to get people out of their cars.

"If we talk about sustainable mobility in general and not only clean public transport, the main problem is the modal shift from private cars to public transport," Le Pira said.

On average, private automobiles account for more than a third of transport in the largest EU capitals, according to CDP data.

Cheaper ticket prices for groups, like students, and disincentives for car use, such as low-emission zones, are two complementary ways of attracting more passengers while reducing private transport.

In her research work, Le Pira investigates how public transport can be more efficient and appealing for city dwellers, for example, by combining transport modes where people step off their bikes and onto a train. This kind of solution could be particularly relevant for small cities "where cars are still the main transport mode."

According to Baierl, places with good public transport draw people in. "Cities where not everybody has to use a car are just more livable," he said.

Edited by: Gianna-Carina Grün and Sarah Steffen

DW's data team contributed research to this project.

For data, code and methodology behind this analysis, see this GitHub repository. More data-driven stories from DW can be found here.

This project is a collaboration among several media outlets in the European Data Journalism Network in context of Chat Europe. Project lead: DW. Contributing partners: Voxeurop, Denik Referendum, EUrologus, OBC Transeuropa.

A very interesting team selection from Andoni Iraola. Liverpool’s head coach had indicated at his pre-match press conference that he was going to go as strong as possible, as his side seek to secure their third straight Champions League win. But the very fact Iraola has chosen to put Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola on the bench indicates he has one eye on Sunday’s demanding assignment against Brighton at Anfield.

Iraola will be delighted to have Cody Gakpo fit again and Lewis Koumas certainly deserves another opportunity to lead the line. But after victory’s against Atletico Madrid and LASK, Liverpool have given themselves some breathing space and it is understandable if Iraola, who has bemoaned the lack of time he has to train his squad, is already plotting Brighton’s downfall.

Your Reds to take on Villarreal in the #UCL! 🔴💫 https://t.co/tlQNFZVMBv

The club known as the “Yellow Submarine” made themselves some fans in the red half of Merseyside by denying Everton a place in the Champions League proper in 2005/06. Everton lost 4-2 on aggregate, and there was controversy in the second leg in Spain when Pierluigi Collina disallowed a Duncan Ferguson header that could have taken the tie to extra time. Everton had finished fourth, one place above Liverpool, the previous season, but Liverpool’s triumph in Istanbul assured them of a qualification place too. Unlike Everton, they prevailed.

Speaking of which, Rafael Benitez is at Anfield this evening.

Dominic King takes stock of Andoni Iraola’s first 10 games in charge of Liverpool and, despite some teething problems, he believes there are reasons to be optimistic. The demands Iraola is putting on Liverpool’s midfielders are an interesting tactical wrinkle, with Dom writing: “Liverpool’s formation will always be written as 4-2-3-1, but the reality is that Iraola’s team do not play in four clear tactical lines. He asks specific jobs of his midfielders, deploying them detailed instructions, and it is going to require some patience before performances become consistent.”

A precious victory at Brentford, Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak among the goals and a couple of improved showings from Florian Wirtz mean things now look a little brighter for Liverpool.

They are strong favourites to make it nine points from nine in the Champions League by beating Villarreal at Anfield this evening, the Spanish club they vanquished in the 2022 semi-finals under Jürgen Klopp.

Liverpool drew Atletico Madrid at home (already ticked off) and Inter Milan away as their two pot-one fixtures, which is about as kind as you can expect. A top-two finish in the league phase is a realistic aspiration for Andoni Iraola’s team, and something would need to go badly awry for them to miss out on the top eight.

Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Isak returned from injury to strengthen Liverpool at Brentford, although Szoboszlai has been lost for a few weeks following another hamstring complication.

Villarreal have punched well above their weight in Europe for the past few decades, reaching two European Cup semi-finals (beaten by Arsenal in 2006 as well as Liverpool in 2022) and winning the Europa League under Unai Emery in 2021.

They have been mediocre in La Liga so far this season though, 12th after nine games on nine points and with a goal difference of zero. Their Champions League performances have been promising though, losing by the odd goal in a frantic finish at Borussia Dortmund and beating Napoli 3-1 at home. Villarreal’s best player is probably Senegalese central midfielder Pape Gueye, and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pépé is also in their ranks. Gueye, despite his position, is their joint-top scorer in all competitions with three goals.

Iraola will be up against his close friend and former Athletic Bilbao team-mate Inigo Perez who is now in charge at Villarreal. Perez was also Iraola’s assistant at Rayo Vallecano, the job which earned the Basque his move to Bournemouth. Perez guided Rayo Vallecano to the Uefa Conference League final last season.

#1193. Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment1,2. Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis3,4,5, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood–brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood–brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin–CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

NEC remains a major cause of mortality and long-term morbidity in preterm infants1,2. NEC pathogenesis is multifactorial, involving the complex interplay of immature intestinal development, intestinal barrier dysfunction, gut dysbiosis and excessive inflammatory response3,4,5,6. The specific triggers of NEC and the mechanisms driving its rapid progression remain poorly understood.

The impact of NEC extends beyond the intestine. More than half of postoperative survivors develop brain injury and neurodevelopmental impairment7,8, with TLR4 inflammatory pathways implicated in this pathology9,10. Many insights are derived from experimental models that use hypoxia, cold stress and hyperosmolar formula feeding to increase intestinal vulnerability11,12. Although these models have been valuable for mapping inflammatory pathways, they may be less well suited to interrogating microbiome-driven early initiating events.

Gut microbiota are implicated in NEC susceptibility: NEC is associated with dysbiosis3,4,5, germ-free mice are resistant to NEC-like injury13 and microbiota-modifying interventions are protective14,15. Several studies identified enrichment of toxin-producing C. perfringens in NEC16,17,18, but causal virulence factors remain undefined.

C. perfringens is a ubiquitous, Gram-positive anaerobe producing diverse toxins19,20. Strains are classified into seven toxin types (A–G) based on toxin repertoire19. Type C strains produce Beta and Delta toxins, which are both pore-forming toxins (PFTs) that induce cell death by forming transmembrane pores21,22,23. While Beta toxin is well characterized, Delta toxin remains understudied. Here we identify C. perfringens Delta toxin as a virulence factor that drives intestinal necrosis and brain injury in a subset of NEC, providing an avenue for targeted therapeutic intervention.

To investigate the role of gut microbiota in NEC, we profiled faecal samples from 28 preterm infants without NEC and 16 preterm infants with NEC. 16S rRNA-sequencing analysis revealed an enrichment of C. perfringens in NEC samples (Fig. 1a), consistent with previous reports16,17. Two fatal cases of NEC showed high C. perfringens abundance (Extended Data Fig. 1a). To validate this finding, we performed anaerobic culture of faecal samples from 49 individuals without NEC and 17 patients with NEC (Supplementary Table 1). C. perfringens-positive cultures showed visible gas production and were confirmed by selective tryptose sulfite cycloserine (TSC) agar isolation and PCR targeting of C. perfringens-specific genes (Extended Data Fig. 1b–d). Overall, C. perfringens was more prevalent in patients with NEC compared with in infants without NEC (56% versus 18%), supporting its association with NEC (Fig. 1b,c).

a, 16S rRNA gene sequencing of faecal samples from infants with (n = 16) and without (n = 28) NEC. b,c, Summary (pie chart (b) and table (c)) of C. perfringens (Cp) and Delta toxin detection across the non-NEC (n = 49) and NEC (n = 27) cohorts as determined by anaerobic culture and serology. d, ELISA detection of anti-Delta toxin antibody in the serum (1:2,700 dilution) of infants without (n = 5) and with (n = 12) NEC. e, Clinical parameter fold changes between the Delta toxin+ (n = 2) and Delta toxin− (n = 5) NEC groups; the blue to magenta gradient indicates the change in magnitude. Mono%, monocyte percentage; T-CO2, total carbon dioxide; Neu%, neutrophil percentage; Lymph%, lymphocyte percentage. f,g, Representative T2W and T2 FLAIR brain MRI scans from the non-NEC (n = 3), Delta toxin− NEC (n = 4) and Delta toxin+ NEC (n = 2) groups (f), and quantification of the Evans index (>0.3 indicates ventricular enlargement) (g). h, Schematic of neonatal mouse NEC model induced by twice-daily intragastric gavage of formula containing C. perfringens. The representative image shows intestinal necrosis in a P11 mouse pup. i,j, Representative intestinal haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining (i) and histopathology scores (j) of pups 4 days after infection with or without C. perfringens. n = 5 (NC), n = 6 (Delta toxin− C. perfringens) and n = 6 (Delta toxin+ C. perfringens). Scale bar, 100 μm. k, Survival curves of pups infected with Delta toxin− or Delta toxin+ C. perfringens. n = 8. l,m, Representative brain H&E staining (l) and quantification of lateral ventricular width (left; n = 4) and ependymal injury scores (right; n = 6) (m) of pups infected with Delta toxin− or Delta toxin+ C. perfringens. Scale bars, 100 μm (top) and 50 μm (bottom). Representative images from one of three independent experiments are shown. Data are mean ± s.d. P values were determined using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA; j and m), two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (g) and the log-rank test (k). *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001. The diagram in h was created using BioRender; Zhang, S. https://BioRender.com/o2lct20 (2026).

C. perfringens produces a repertoire of toxins, including Alpha, Beta, Epsilon, Iota toxin, enterotoxin (CPE), necrotic enteritis β-like toxin (NetB) and perfringolysin O (Pfo)19. We next examined whether specific toxin profiles correlated with severe outcomes. PCR-based toxin typing identified isolates from two deceased patients as type C C. perfringens strains containing the delta toxin gene (Delta toxin+ C. perfringens clinical-03 and clinical-15) (Extended Data Fig. 1e). Delta toxin production was further confirmed by western blot analysis of culture supernatants (Extended Data Fig. 1f,g). We further detected anti-Delta toxin antibodies in two patients with severe surgical NEC whose stool cultures were negative, probably due to antibiotic treatment, indicating previous infection with Delta toxin+ C. perfringens strains. Expanded serological analysis of ten additional patients with severe surgical NEC identified five anti-Delta toxin antibody-positive cases (Supplementary Table 2). Thus, 7 of 12 (58%) patients with severe NEC showed serological evidence of Delta toxin exposure, whereas Delta toxin was not detected in any infant without NEC by faecal isolate PCR or serology (Fig. 1b–d).

Clinically, Delta toxin+ infants showed more prominent systemic inflammation, coagulopathy and brain injury, compared with Delta toxin− cases characterized by elevated C-reactive protein and D-dimer, decreased monocytes, platelets and haemoglobin (Fig. 1e). Importantly, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in these patients indicated more severe injury, including lateral ventricular enlargement (Fig. 1f,g).

To assess Delta toxin pathogenicity, we selected representative clinical isolates, the Delta toxin+ strain C. perfringens clinical-03 and the Delta toxin− strain C. perfringens clinical-01 for genomic analysis and animal infection studies (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f). Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the clinical-03 strain clustered with NCTC3181 (a known Delta toxin+ type C strain24), whereas clinical-01 clustered with CVCC1160 (a Delta toxin− type C strain), with the two clinical isolates sharing around 96% DNA identity (Extended Data Fig. 1h). Neonatal mice orally gavaged with these strains and formula for 4 days developed severe NEC-like intestinal pathology only after Delta toxin+ infection, including disrupted intestinal architecture, villus and crypt damage, inflammatory infiltration and mucosal fibrin clots, accompanied by increased mortality (Fig. 1h–k). During infection with the clinical-03 strain, Delta toxin was detected predominantly in the intestine, with lower levels in the kidney and lung, but was undetectable in the brain based on western blotting and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (Extended Data Fig. 1i,j). Nevertheless, infected mice developed severe brain abnormalities, including lateral ventricular enlargement and ependymal cell damage (Fig. 1l,m). Reference strain comparison using NCTC3181 and CVCC1160 (around 99% identity) confirmed that Delta toxin+ infection caused more severe intestinal, brain and lung injury (Extended Data Fig. 1k–m). Finally, culture supernatants from Delta toxin+ strains induced cytotoxicity in HeLa cells, HT29 cells and intestinal organoids, which was neutralized by a Delta-toxin-specific polyclonal antibody (Extended Data Fig. 1n–p). These results support Delta toxin as a key secreted virulence factor responsible for cell damage.

Owing to technical challenges in performing some assays in postnatal day 7 (P7) neonatal mice, we included 4-week-old weanling mice for subsequent experiments. Intraperitoneal (i.p.) administration of purified Delta toxin caused dose-dependent lethality in both age groups, with neonates showing greater sensitivity (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 2a). We next quantified Delta toxin distribution in neonatal mice 4 h after i.p. injection of 10 μg toxin. Consistent with the infection model, toxin levels were highest in the intestine (around 61 μg per g), followed by kidney (approximately 15 μg per g) and lung (about 7 μg per g), with barely detectable toxin in the brain (Extended Data Fig. 2b). These levels were comparable to those in infected pups, supporting the physiological relevance of the toxin injection model.

We next challenged P7 neonates and 4-week-old mice using either an acute high-dose model to mimic fulminant infection, analysed at 4 h, or a single low-dose challenge with prolonged follow-up to approximate residual toxin activity after antibiotic clearance, analysed at days 5–7. Across both age groups and dosing strategies, Delta toxin induced a severe NEC-like multiorgan pathology. Intestines showed mucosal disruption, villus destruction, epithelial detachment and oedema (Fig. 2c,d and Extended Data Fig. 2c,d). Concurrently, the brain exhibited haemorrhage, ependymal disorganization, periventricular oedema, ventricular dilation (Fig. 2e,f and Extended Data Fig. 2e,f), neuronal shrinkage and degeneration, and inflammatory cell infiltration (Fig. 2g,h and Extended Data Fig. 2g–i). We also observed intravascular coagulation within the cerebral microvasculature in the hippocampal region (Extended Data Fig. 2j,k). In 4-week-old mice, brain MRI further confirmed that Delta toxin caused brain injury and ventricle dilation (Fig. 2i,j), mirroring the neuropathology observed in patients with NEC. In vivo photoacoustic imaging of brains showed a significant reduction in cerebral blood flow, vascular density and branching index, indicating Delta-toxin-associated hypoxic–ischaemic injury and cognitive impairment (Fig. 2k,l).

Beyond the brain, Delta toxin induced widespread multiorgan pathology, with particularly severe injury observed in the kidney and lung. These tissues exhibited distinct signs of coagulopathy, haemorrhage and inflammatory cell infiltration, notably affecting the renal medulla, glomeruli and pulmonary parenchyma in both age groups (Extended Data Fig. 2l–o). Moreover, toxin-treated mice showed dilated ear vessels and increased Evans blue extravasation in the peritoneal lavage fluid, indicating vascular damage25 (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). Delta toxin further induced systemic coagulation abnormalities, including elevated red blood cell counts, reduced platelets and altered coagulation parameters, including prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time,  and reduced fibrinogen (Extended Data Fig. 3c–h). These findings recapitulate the severe disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) observed in Delta-toxin-positive patients with NEC (Fig. 1e). Inflammasome activation is known to drive coagulation through macrophage-mediated release of tissue factor26. Consistently, Delta toxin promoted tissue factor release from macrophages and Caco2 intestinal epithelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 3i), suggesting that both cell types contribute to toxin-induced coagulopathy.

To define the specific contribution of Delta toxin to neurological injury, we evaluated the effects of Beta toxin, which has been implicated in type C C. perfringens enteritis27. Beta toxin exhibited selective cytotoxicity for endothelial HUVECs but notably spared HT-29 intestinal epithelial cells and organoids (Extended Data Fig. 4a–c), aligning with a previous report that Beta toxin preferentially targets CD31+ vascular endothelial cells28. In vivo, it induced rapid, dose-dependent mortality (Extended Data Fig. 4d), but did not induce brain pathology at any dose tested (Extended Data Fig. 4e). These data demonstrate the specific pathogenic role of Delta toxin as a driver of NEC-like multiorgan pathology.

We next examined whether Delta-toxin-induced brain injury is associated with blood–brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction and neuroinflammation. In 4-week-old mice, Evans blue extravasation revealed dose-dependent BBB leakage after Delta toxin challenge, with lipopolysaccharide (LPS)29 as a positive control (Fig. 2m–o). Acute high-dose Delta toxin (100 μg, 8 h) caused more-severe BBB disruption than either prolonged low-dose Delta toxin (20 μg, analysed at day 7) or acute LPS (1 mg, 8 h), indicating that Delta toxin rapidly disrupts BBB integrity. ZO-1 immunofluorescence in the hippocampus confirmed structural damage with localized disorganization and reduced signal intensity (Fig. 2p,q).

BBB disruption is often accompanied by neuroinflammation30,31 and intestinal CD4+ T cells migrate across the BBB into the brain, where they accumulate with microglia to trigger neuroinflammation32,33. We next characterized brain immune cell populations after exposure to Delta toxin. In both age groups, acute high-dose Delta toxin triggered an increase in total CD45+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 5a). This increase was largely attributable to a marked expansion of the microglial population, predominantly reflecting microglial expansion (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c), confirmed by increased IBA1+ immunostaining (Extended Data Fig. 5d–g). Three-dimensional analysis revealed a shift of microglia from ramified to amoeboid morphology, characterized by shorter branch lengths and attenuated processes (Extended Data Fig. 5d–g). GFAP+ astrocytes also increased, with increased branching and cell volume (Extended Data Fig. 5h–k), indicating pro-inflammatory activation34. CD4+ and CD8+ T cells remained at similar levels at this timepoint (Extended Data Fig. 5l). In neonates after low-dose prolonged challenge, microglial expansion and activation (Extended Data Fig. 5m–r) were accompanied by increased CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Extended Data Fig. 5s,t), consistent with T cell recruitment 4 days after NEC induction32.

As patients with NEC exhibit a pronounced systemic and central nervous system inflammatory response1, we analysed cytokine profiles in the serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients with NEC positive for C. perfringens Delta toxin. The results revealed abnormally high cytokine levels, including IL-6, IL-10, TNF and IL-1β (Fig. 3a,b). To examine whether Delta toxin contributes to this inflammatory activation, we administered Delta toxin to 4-week-old mice through i.p. injection and observed a significant increase in IL-1β levels in both the serum and peritoneal fluid (Fig. 3c), along with a dose-dependent upregulation of Il1b, Il18, Tnf and Nlrp3 mRNA levels in peritoneal lavage cells (Fig. 3d). IL-1β and IL-18 are major effector cytokines released after NLRP3 inflammasome activation35, and activated macrophages represent the principal cellular source of mature IL-1β36. The specific NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950 suppressed Delta-toxin-induced Il1b and Il18 in peritoneal macrophages (Fig. 3e), improved survival rates (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6a) and mitigated Delta-toxin-induced BBB disruption, as evidenced by reduced Evans blue extravasation (Fig. 3g,h). These findings suggest that Delta toxin activates the NLRP3 inflammasome to drive local and systemic inflammation as well as BBB damage.

We next examined whether macrophages, well-established cells capable of NLRP3 inflammasome activation, are preferentially targeted by Delta toxin. In both neonates and 4-week-old mice, high-dose Delta toxin caused rapid, near-complete depletion of peritoneal macrophages within 1 h, and low-dose exposure resulted in reduced peritoneal macrophage numbers persisting for 5–7 days (Fig. 3i,j and Extended Data Fig. 6b–d). By contrast, neutrophils decreased at 1 h, accumulated by 4 h and persisted to days 5–7, suggesting a subsequent neutrophil-dominated inflammatory response (Fig. 3i,j and Extended Data Fig. 6b–d). In the neonatal intestine, Delta toxin selectively depleted macrophages, without significantly altering T cells, B cells, neutrophils or dendritic cells (Fig. 3k,l and Extended Data Fig. 6e,f). Consistently, neonatal mice infected with the NCTC3181 (Delta toxin+) strain showed both a reduced percentage and a reduced absolute number of intestinal macrophages at 4 days after infection, whereas infection with the CVCC1160 strain (Delta toxin−) resulted in no detectable change (Fig. 3m). To assess the inflammatory potency relative to other PFTs, we exposed primary peritoneal macrophages to Staphylococcus aureus α-haemolysin (α-Hla), C. perfringens Delta toxin, Beta toxin, Pfo or LPS. Macrophages were resistant to α-Hla, Beta toxin and Pfo, but exceptionally sensitive to Delta toxin (Fig. 3n). Delta toxin potently induced inflammatory cytokine mRNA at 1–5 ng ml−1, whereas Pfo and α-Hla required around 5,000 ng ml−1 and 50,000 ng ml−1, respectively; Beta toxin had a minimal effect even at high concentrations. Notably, Delta toxin was effective at approximately 100-fold lower concentrations than LPS (Fig. 3o). Consistently, IL-1β was detected in primary peritoneal macrophage culture supernatants after 10 ng ml−1 Delta toxin treatment (Fig. 3p).

To define the mechanism, we examined key inflammatory cell-death pathways in immortalized bone-marrow-derived macrophages (iBMDMs). Delta toxin induced a time-dependent increase in pyroptosis signatures, including accumulation of pro-caspase-1, cleaved caspase-1 and gasdermin D (Fig. 3q). By contrast, canonical apoptosis markers, BAX induction and caspase-3 cleavage37 were not detectably altered under the same conditions (Fig. 3r), supporting pyroptosis as the dominant cell-death program induced by Delta toxin in iBMDMs.

We next tested whether K+ efflux38, a conserved trigger for NLRP3 inflammasome activation after membrane permeabilization, mediates Delta-toxin-induced inflammation. Extracellular KCl, used to prevent intracellular K+ depletion, abrogated Delta-toxin-induced NLRP3 upregulation and caspase-1 cleavage (Extended Data Fig. 6g), identifying K+ efflux as a major upstream signal. Moreover, Delta toxin rapidly induced ERK phosphorylation (Fig. 3s), consistent with pore-forming toxin-induced calcium influx, which subsequently activates MAPK–ERK signalling39. In vivo, bone marrow cells from Delta-toxin-treated mice showed increased GSDMD cleavage (Fig. 3t), confirming pyroptotic signalling. Collectively, these findings reveal that Delta toxin drives potent inflammation through the NLRP3–Caspase-1–GSDMD pathway and activates MAPK–ERK signalling.

We next examined whether Delta toxin engages a specific host receptor to mediate cell binding and cytotoxicity. We first evaluated the sensitivity of various cell lines. HeLa and HT29 cells were found to be highly susceptible, indicating that they abundantly express receptor (Extended Data Fig. 7a). We therefore performed a genome-wide CRISPR–Cas9 screen in HeLa cells using the GeCKO v2 library40 against Delta toxin (0.01 μg ml−1) (Fig. 4a). Next-generation sequencing of surviving cells revealed Cd9 as the top hit (Fig. 4b). CD9 expression was confirmed across relevant cell lines, and higher CD9 expression was associated with increased sensitivity to Delta toxin (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 7a). Although Delta toxin has been reported to bind to GM221, genetic disruption (UGCG knockout (KO)) or pharmacological inhibition (EtDO-P4 treatment) of GlcCer-derived glycosphingolipids (including most gangliosides such as GM2) did not change cellular sensitivity (Extended Data Fig. 7b,c). By contrast, CD9-KO rendered HeLa cells resistant to Delta toxin with toxicity reduced by around 40,000-fold (Fig. 4d). Moreover, CD9-overexpressing (CD9-GFP-oe) A549 cells showed markedly increased sensitivity (Fig. 4e). KO of other candidate genes (LRP6 and CLEC12B) did not alter toxin sensitivity (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 7d). GST-tagged Delta toxin can bind to wild-type (WT) HeLa cells and CD9-GFP-oe A549 cells, but not to CD9-KO cells and A549 cells (Fig. 4f–h). Biolayer interferometry (BLI) assays confirmed specific binding between GST–CD9 and Delta toxin, but not Beta toxin (Fig. 4i). The measured interaction (KD) fell in the micromolar-range binding affinity, indicative of specific, low-affinity binding (Extended Data Fig. 7e,f). It is possible that a proper membrane environment is required for the high-affinity binding of Delta toxin on cell surfaces. Together, these data identify CD9 as a receptor for Delta toxin.
